claim: Inhibitory autapses are self-innervating synaptic connections in GABAergic interneurons in the brain.
source: Inhibitory autapses are self-innervating synaptic connections in GABAergic interneurons in the brain.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes what autapses are.

claim: Autapses in neocortical layers have not been systematically investigated.
source: Autapses in neocortical layers have not been systematically investigated, and their function in different mammalian species and specific interneuron types is poorly known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: Most pvBCs showed robust GABAAR-mediated self-innervation in both human and mouse species.
source: Most pvBCs showed robust GABAAR-mediated self-innervation in both species, but autapses were rare in nonfast-spiking GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Autapses were rare in nonfast-spiking GABAergic interneurons.
source: Most pvBCs showed robust GABAAR-mediated self-innervation in both species, but autapses were rare in nonfast-spiking GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data comparing pvBCs to nonFSINs.

claim: Light- and electron microscopy analyses revealed pvBC axons innervating their own soma and proximal dendrites.
source: Light- and electron microscopy analyses revealed pvBC axons innervating their own soma and proximal dendrites.
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance was similar in human and mouse pvBCs.
source: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance was similar in human and mouse pvBCs and comparable to that of synapses from pvBCs to other L2/3 neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological measurements comparing species.

claim: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance in pvBCs was comparable to that of synapses from pvBCs to other L2/3 neurons.
source: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance was similar in human and mouse pvBCs and comparable to that of synapses from pvBCs to other L2/3 neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological measurements comparing autaptic and synaptic conductances.

claim: Autaptic conductance prolonged somatic inhibition in pvBCs after a spike.
source: Autaptic conductance prolonged somatic inhibition in pvBCs after a spike and inhibited repetitive firing.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological experiments examining the functional effects of autapses.

claim: Autaptic conductance inhibited repetitive firing in pvBCs.
source: Autaptic conductance prolonged somatic inhibition in pvBCs after a spike and inhibited repetitive firing.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological experiments examining the functional effects of autapses.

claim: Perisomatic autaptic inhibition is common in both human and mouse pvBCs of supragranular neocortex.
source: Perisomatic autaptic inhibition is common in both human and mouse pvBCs of supragranular neocortex, where they efficiently control discharge of the pvBCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Perisomatic autaptic inhibition efficiently controls discharge of pvBCs.
source: Perisomatic autaptic inhibition is common in both human and mouse pvBCs of supragranular neocortex, where they efficiently control discharge of the pvBCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional experiments showing effects on firing.

claim: Autapses are synapses made by a neuron onto itself.
source: Autapses are synapses made by a neuron onto itself (Bekkers, 2003; Deleuze et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies on experimental animals have reported autaptic self-innervation in some inhibitory as well as in excitatory neurons in the brain.
source: Although studies on experimental animals have reported autaptic self-innervation in some inhibitory as well as in excitatory neurons in the brain, (Karabelas and Purpura, 1980; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson et al., 1996; Cobb et al., 1997; Pouzat and Marty, 1998; Bacci et al., 2003; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Karayannis et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2018), little is known about autapses in human nerve cells, and only a single study has investigated the operation of autaptic self-inhibition in the human neocortex (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior literature with multiple citations.

claim: Little is known about autapses in human nerve cells.
source: Although studies on experimental animals have reported autaptic self-innervation in some inhibitory as well as in excitatory neurons in the brain, (Karabelas and Purpura, 1980; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson et al., 1996; Cobb et al., 1997; Pouzat and Marty, 1998; Bacci et al., 2003; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Karayannis et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2018), little is known about autapses in human nerve cells, and only a single study has investigated the operation of autaptic self-inhibition in the human neocortex (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature regarding human autapses.

claim: Only a single study has investigated the operation of autaptic self-inhibition in the human neocortex.
source: Although studies on experimental animals have reported autaptic self-innervation in some inhibitory as well as in excitatory neurons in the brain, (Karabelas and Purpura, 1980; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson et al., 1996; Cobb et al., 1997; Pouzat and Marty, 1998; Bacci et al., 2003; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Karayannis et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2018), little is known about autapses in human nerve cells, and only a single study has investigated the operation of autaptic self-inhibition in the human neocortex (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2012.

claim: In layer 5 of the infragranular neocortex, GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition prolongs the pvBC spiking interval during sustained high-frequency firing.
source: In layer 5 of the infragranular neocortex, GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition prolongs the pvBC spiking interval during sustained high-frequency firing (Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Manseau et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Evidence for autapses exists in the human epileptic infragranular neocortex, where high-frequency spike bursts are associated with autaptic GABA release from fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Evidence for autapses also exists in the human epileptic infragranular neocortex, where high-frequency spike bursts are associated with autaptic GABA release from fast-spiking interneurons (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2012.

claim: The operation of autaptic self-inhibition in superficial neocortical layers is unknown.
source: However, the operation of autaptic self-inhibition in superficial neocortical layers is unknown (Tamás et al., 1997).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: GABAergic inhibition at the perisomatic region efficiently controls spike output.
source: GABAergic inhibition at the perisomatic region efficiently controls spike output (Tremblay et al., 2016; Feldmeyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: pvBCs are key players synchronizing neuronal network activity through their inhibitory synapses.
source: Hence, pvBCs are key players synchronizing neuronal network activity through their inhibitory synapses (Cobb et al., 1995; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Wood et al., 2017; Cardin, 2018), and altered pvBC firing is often linked to pathological network activities (Jiang et al., 2016; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Dienel and Lewis, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Altered pvBC firing is often linked to pathological network activities.
source: Hence, pvBCs are key players synchronizing neuronal network activity through their inhibitory synapses (Cobb et al., 1995; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Wood et al., 2017; Cardin, 2018), and altered pvBC firing is often linked to pathological network activities (Jiang et al., 2016; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Dienel and Lewis, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Perisomatic inhibition through autapses can efficiently regulate pvBC firing.
source: In addition, perisomatic inhibition through autapses can efficiently regulate pvBC firing (Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Guo et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Computational models can help us understand the role of pvBC self-inhibition in the generation and maintenance of cortical network activities.
source: Computational models can help us understand the role of pvBC self-inhibition in the generation and maintenance of cortical network activities (Connelly, 2014; Guo et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2016), but very little is known about autapses in human brain, including their occurrence and inhibitory efficacy in distinct interneuron types.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: Very little is known about autapses in human brain, including their occurrence and inhibitory efficacy in distinct interneuron types.
source: Computational models can help us understand the role of pvBC self-inhibition in the generation and maintenance of cortical network activities (Connelly, 2014; Guo et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2016), but very little is known about autapses in human brain, including their occurrence and inhibitory efficacy in distinct interneuron types.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: The study investigated GABAergic autapses in human and mouse supragranular layer 2/3 pvBCs and some nonfast-spiking interneurons.
source: We investigated GABAergic autapses in human and mouse supragranular layer 2/3 pvBCs and some nonfast-spiking interneurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: GABAAR-mediated inhibition is present in most pvBCs in both human and mouse species.
source: We show that GABAAR-mediated inhibition is present in most pvBCs in both species and that perisomatic autaptic contacts in these interneurons suppress excitability and inhibit repetitive firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Perisomatic autaptic contacts in pvBCs suppress excitability and inhibit repetitive firing.
source: We show that GABAAR-mediated inhibition is present in most pvBCs in both species and that perisomatic autaptic contacts in these interneurons suppress excitability and inhibit repetitive firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: GABAergic interneuron autapses are a standard and cell type-specific microcircuit feature in the mammalian neocortex.
source: We conclude that GABAergic interneuron autapses are a standard and cell type-specific microcircuit feature in the mammalian neocortex that mediates strong perisomatic self-inhibition of pvBCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: GABAergic interneuron autapses mediate strong perisomatic self-inhibition of pvBCs.
source: We conclude that GABAergic interneuron autapses are a standard and cell type-specific microcircuit feature in the mammalian neocortex that mediates strong perisomatic self-inhibition of pvBCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The study investigated 46 supragranular layer 2/3 pvBCs in human neocortical tissue.
source: We investigated autapses in 46 supragranular layer 2/3 (L2/3) pvBCs and 22 nonfast spiking interneurons (nonFSINs) in human neocortical tissue resected from frontal, temporal or occipital areas during deep brain surgery to obtain access to subcortical pathological targets (tumor, cyst, aneurysm or catheter implant).
evidence: This describes the sample size and source of human tissue.

claim: The study investigated 22 nonfast spiking interneurons in human neocortical tissue.
source: We investigated autapses in 46 supragranular layer 2/3 (L2/3) pvBCs and 22 nonfast spiking interneurons (nonFSINs) in human neocortical tissue resected from frontal, temporal or occipital areas during deep brain surgery to obtain access to subcortical pathological targets (tumor, cyst, aneurysm or catheter implant).
evidence: This describes the sample size of nonFSINs studied.

claim: Human neocortical tissue was resected from frontal, temporal or occipital areas during deep brain surgery.
source: We investigated autapses in 46 supragranular layer 2/3 (L2/3) pvBCs and 22 nonfast spiking interneurons (nonFSINs) in human neocortical tissue resected from frontal, temporal or occipital areas during deep brain surgery to obtain access to subcortical pathological targets (tumor, cyst, aneurysm or catheter implant).
evidence: This describes the source and method of obtaining human tissue.

claim: 39 basket cells were identified by their axon forming boutons around unlabeled L2/3 neurons.
source: 39 basket cells were identified by their axon forming boutons around unlabeled L2/3 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Szegedi et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the anatomical identification method for basket cells.

claim: Seven unsuccessfully visualized fast-spiking interneurons were included as putative pvBCs.
source: Seven unsuccessfully visualized fast-spiking interneurons were included as putative pvBCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the classification of cells that could not be fully visualized.

claim: In 11 of 13 pvBCs studied, unitary spikes triggered GABAAR-mediated depolarizing potentials with high intracellular chloride.
source: Under these conditions, unitary spikes (interval 10 s) in 11 of the 13 pvBCs studied triggered GABAAR-mediated depolarizing potentials (5.44 ± 0.73 mV peak amplitude, p=0.380, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11), showing a 0.92 ± 0.04 ms onset delay to the preceding action potential peak (p=0.132, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11) (see Figure 1aii).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings with elevated intracellular chloride.

claim: Autaptic depolarizing potentials in pvBCs had a peak amplitude of 5.44 ± 0.73 mV.
source: Under these conditions, unitary spikes (interval 10 s) in 11 of the 13 pvBCs studied triggered GABAAR-mediated depolarizing potentials (5.44 ± 0.73 mV peak amplitude, p=0.380, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11), showing a 0.92 ± 0.04 ms onset delay to the preceding action potential peak (p=0.132, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11) (see Figure 1aii).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Autaptic depolarizing potentials in pvBCs showed a 0.92 ± 0.04 ms onset delay to the preceding action potential peak.
source: Under these conditions, unitary spikes (interval 10 s) in 11 of the 13 pvBCs studied triggered GABAAR-mediated depolarizing potentials (5.44 ± 0.73 mV peak amplitude, p=0.380, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11), showing a 0.92 ± 0.04 ms onset delay to the preceding action potential peak (p=0.132, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11) (see Figure 1aii).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: NonFSINs showed gabazine-sensitive autaptic potentials in only 1 of 14 cells studied.
source: In contrast, nonFSINs (action potential inward current width 0.886 ± 0.036 ms vs. 0.536 ± 0.024 ms in pvBCs, p=0.001, Student's t-test) showed gabazine (GBZ)-sensitive autaptic potentials in only 1 of the 14 cells studied.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings comparing nonFSINs to pvBCs.

claim: NonFSINs have an action potential inward current width of 0.886 ± 0.036 ms.
source: In contrast, nonFSINs (action potential inward current width 0.886 ± 0.036 ms vs. 0.536 ± 0.024 ms in pvBCs, p=0.001, Student's t-test) showed gabazine (GBZ)-sensitive autaptic potentials in only 1 of the 14 cells studied.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: pvBCs have an action potential inward current width of 0.536 ± 0.024 ms.
source: In contrast, nonFSINs (action potential inward current width 0.886 ± 0.036 ms vs. 0.536 ± 0.024 ms in pvBCs, p=0.001, Student's t-test) showed gabazine (GBZ)-sensitive autaptic potentials in only 1 of the 14 cells studied.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The autaptic response was readily blocked by gabazine (10 μM).
source: The autaptic response was readily blocked by GBZ (10 μM) (p<0.001, n = 5) (Figure 1ci, ii) or gradually abolished by intracellular calcium-chelator BAPTA (20 mM), which suppresses action potential-dependent vesicle release (p<0.001, n = 6) (Wilcoxon signed rank test) (Figure 1di, ii) (Bacci et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The autaptic response was gradually abolished by intracellular calcium-chelator BAPTA (20 mM).
source: The autaptic response was readily blocked by GBZ (10 μM) (p<0.001, n = 5) (Figure 1ci, ii) or gradually abolished by intracellular calcium-chelator BAPTA (20 mM), which suppresses action potential-dependent vesicle release (p<0.001, n = 6) (Wilcoxon signed rank test) (Figure 1di, ii) (Bacci et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: BAPTA suppresses action potential-dependent vesicle release.
source: The autaptic response was readily blocked by GBZ (10 μM) (p<0.001, n = 5) (Figure 1ci, ii) or gradually abolished by intracellular calcium-chelator BAPTA (20 mM), which suppresses action potential-dependent vesicle release (p<0.001, n = 6) (Wilcoxon signed rank test) (Figure 1di, ii) (Bacci et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a known property of BAPTA supported by citation.

claim: Electron microscopic investigation revealed pvBC biocytin-filled axon terminal boutons forming contacts to their own soma and proximal dendrites.
source: The analysis in two cells showing electrophysiological evidence for GABAergic autapses revealed pvBC biocytin-filled axon terminal boutons forming contacts to their own soma (1 and 4 contacts) and proximal dendrites (1 and 2 contacts), revealing postautaptic density in the neuron (Figure 1bi–iii).
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In human pvBCs, a spike-evoked autaptic response showed peak Gaut of 3.79 nS (median, quartiles 2.39–6.45 nS, n = 14 cells).
source: In human pvBCs, a spike-evoked autaptic response showed peak Gaut of 3.79 nS, 2.39–6.45 nS (median, quartiles, n = 14 cells) and 4.18 ± 0.31 ms decay time constant (p=0.829, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 13 cells, monoexponential curve fitting r2 range from 0.86 to 0.97. A pvBC with smallest Gaut amplitude was excluded from the decay tau analysis).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: Human pvBC autaptic responses had a decay time constant of 4.18 ± 0.31 ms.
source: In human pvBCs, a spike-evoked autaptic response showed peak Gaut of 3.79 nS, 2.39–6.45 nS (median, quartiles, n = 14 cells) and 4.18 ± 0.31 ms decay time constant (p=0.829, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 13 cells, monoexponential curve fitting r2 range from 0.86 to 0.97. A pvBC with smallest Gaut amplitude was excluded from the decay tau analysis).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: The autaptic current peak amplitude had a 2.31 ± 0.16 ms delay to the action potential inward current peak.
source: The autaptic current peak amplitude had a 2.31 ± 0.16 ms (p=0.066, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 13) delay to the action potential inward current peak.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: GBZ-sensitive autapses were confirmed in 25 of 36 (69.4%) human pvBCs studied.
source: Altogether, experiments including the current- and voltage clamp measurements above confirmed GBZ-sensitive autapses in 25 of 36 (69.4 %) human pvBCs studied (see Figure 2aii), showing no difference in patient age between pvBCs with or without autapses (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, D = 0.200 with p=0.884).
evidence: This is a summary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: There was no difference in patient age between pvBCs with or without autapses.
source: Altogether, experiments including the current- and voltage clamp measurements above confirmed GBZ-sensitive autapses in 25 of 36 (69.4 %) human pvBCs studied (see Figure 2aii), showing no difference in patient age between pvBCs with or without autapses (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, D = 0.200 with p=0.884).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of patient demographics.

claim: There was no correlation between autapse peak conductance and patient age.
source: There was no correlation between autapse peak conductance and patient age (Spearman's r = −0.142, p=0.615, n = 14).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between autapse properties and patient age.

claim: The human pvBC autapse peak conductance was not different from synaptic conductance tested in 20 monosynaptically connected pvBC-PC pairs.
source: On average, the human pvBC autapse peak conductance was not different from synaptic conductance (Gsyn) tested in 20 monosynaptically connected pvBC-PC pairs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and it was comparable to monosynaptic conductance between pvBCs (average synaptic conductance in BC-BC three pairs; 1.04 nS, 1.68 nS and 1.84 nS).
evidence: This is a comparison of autaptic and synaptic conductances from paired recordings.

claim: Synaptic GABAAR-mediated peak conductance in pvBC-PC pairs was 3.10 nS (median, quartiles 1.42–3.94 nS).
source: Synaptic GABAAR-mediated peak conductance was 3.10 nS, 1.42–3.94 nS (median, quartiles) (p=0.128, Mann–Whitney U -test compared to Gaut in humans).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired recordings.

claim: GBZ-sensitive autapses were found in 11 of 19 mouse pvBCs, representing 57.9% of the cells studied.
source: We found GBZ-sensitive autapses in 11 of 19 mouse pvBCs, representing 57.9% of the cells studied (Figure 2bii, iii).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings in mouse.

claim: Mouse pvBCs had Gaut peaks of 4.09 nS (median, quartiles 1.93–5.67 nS, n = 11).
source: Mouse pvBCs (n = 11) had Gaut peaks of 4.09 nS, 1.93–5.67 nS, akin to what we discovered in human pvBCs (p=0.72, Mann–Whitney U -test) (Figure 2ci).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings in mouse.

claim: Mouse pvBC autaptic conductance was similar to human pvBC autaptic conductance.
source: Mouse pvBCs (n = 11) had Gaut peaks of 4.09 nS, 1.93–5.67 nS, akin to what we discovered in human pvBCs (p=0.72, Mann–Whitney U -test) (Figure 2ci).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: Mouse pvBC autaptic current decay time constant was 3.91 ms (median, quartiles 3.55–6.47 ms, n = 11).
source: Autaptic current decay time constant defined by monoexponential curve fitting was 3.91 ms, 3.55–6.47 ms (n = 11).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings in mouse.

claim: Mouse pvBC input resistance was 139.60 ± 6.69 MΩ.
source: Mouse pvBC input resistance under resting conditions (139.60 ± 6.69 MΩ, p=0.566, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) was not significantly different from Rm in human pvBCs (183.83 ± 22.34 MΩ, p=0.247, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 14) (p=0.077, Welch's t-test), but compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs showed a wide Rm value range (D = 0.500, p=0.060, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (see Figure 2cii).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings in mouse.

claim: Human pvBC input resistance was 183.83 ± 22.34 MΩ.
source: Mouse pvBC input resistance under resting conditions (139.60 ± 6.69 MΩ, p=0.566, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) was not significantly different from Rm in human pvBCs (183.83 ± 22.34 MΩ, p=0.247, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 14) (p=0.077, Welch's t-test), but compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs showed a wide Rm value range (D = 0.500, p=0.060, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (see Figure 2cii).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological recordings in human.

claim: Mouse pvBC input resistance was not significantly different from human pvBC input resistance.
source: Mouse pvBC input resistance under resting conditions (139.60 ± 6.69 MΩ, p=0.566, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) was not significantly different from Rm in human pvBCs (183.83 ± 22.34 MΩ, p=0.247, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 14) (p=0.077, Welch's t-test), but compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs showed a wide Rm value range (D = 0.500, p=0.060, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (see Figure 2cii).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: Human pvBCs showed a wide Rm value range compared to mouse pvBCs.
source: Mouse pvBC input resistance under resting conditions (139.60 ± 6.69 MΩ, p=0.566, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) was not significantly different from Rm in human pvBCs (183.83 ± 22.34 MΩ, p=0.247, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 14) (p=0.077, Welch's t-test), but compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs showed a wide Rm value range (D = 0.500, p=0.060, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (see Figure 2cii).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of data distributions between species.

claim: Human and mouse pvBCs exhibited comparable Gaut+leak/Gleak values.
source: On average, human and mouse pvBCs exhibited comparable Gaut+leak/Gleak values (p=0.985 Shapiro-Wilk normality test; p=0.358 vs. human, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: Human pvBCs showed a peak Gahp of 17.48 ± 1.81 nS.
source: Human pvBCs showed a peak Gahp of 17.48 ± 1.81 nS (p=0.445, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) measured from the AHP current peak in the presence of GBZ (peak at 0.78 ± 0.06 ms delay to the action inward current peak, p=0.066, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) (n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: The AHP outward current decay time constant from the peak in human pvBCs was 5.43 ± 0.54 ms.
source: The AHP outward current decay time constant from the peak was 5.43 ± 0.54 ms (p=0.190, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: The Gahp peak amplitude correlated with cell capacitance in human pvBCs.
source: The variability in the Gahp peak amplitude between individual pvBCs probably reflects the cell soma size since the peak Gahp value correlated with the cell capacitance (Cm = 43.81, 27.65–58.60 pF, n = 14) (Spearman's r = 0.644, p=0.012, n = 14) and Gleak (Pearson's r = 0.671, p=0.009, n = 14).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The Gahp peak amplitude correlated with Gleak in human pvBCs.
source: The variability in the Gahp peak amplitude between individual pvBCs probably reflects the cell soma size since the peak Gahp value correlated with the cell capacitance (Cm = 43.81, 27.65–58.60 pF, n = 14) (Spearman's r = 0.644, p=0.012, n = 14) and Gleak (Pearson's r = 0.671, p=0.009, n = 14).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Cm or Gleak failed to show correlation with peak Gaut in human pvBCs.
source: However, Cm or Gleak failed to show correlation with peak Gaut (Spearman's test) (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The mouse Gahp peak amplitude was 25.21 ± 2.60 nS.
source: The mouse Gahp peak amplitude was 25.21 ± 2.60 nS (p=0.096, n = 11) and the peak showed 0.59 ± 0.068 ms (p=0.312, n = 11) delay to the action inward current peak (Shapiro-Wilk normality test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings in mouse.

claim: The AHP current in mouse pvBCs had decay time constant of 2.91 ± 0.26 ms.
source: The AHP current had decay time constant of 2.91 ± 0.26 ms (p=0.109, Shapiro-Wilk normality test, n = 11).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from voltage clamp recordings in mouse.

claim: The Gahp peak amplitude in mouse cells was higher than that in human pvBCs.
source: Thus, the Gahp peak amplitude in mouse cells was higher than that in human pvBCs (p=0.007, Student's t-test), and the AHP current in mice was shorter than that in humans (decay tau mean 2.91 ms vs. 5.43 ms, p=0.002, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: The AHP current in mice was shorter than that in humans.
source: Thus, the Gahp peak amplitude in mouse cells was higher than that in human pvBCs (p=0.007, Student's t-test), and the AHP current in mice was shorter than that in humans (decay tau mean 2.91 ms vs. 5.43 ms, p=0.002, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: Simulation results demonstrate effective self-inhibition of EPSP amplitude by GABAA receptor-mediated autaptic conductance for ten milliseconds following a spike.
source: The results demonstrate effective self-inhibition of the EPSP amplitude by GABAA receptor-mediated autaptic conductance for ten milliseconds following a spike.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling experiments.

claim: Wash-in of GBZ selectively increased the postspike EPSP amplitude in pvBCs to 119.6 ± 3.3% from baseline.
source: Following baseline, wash-in of GBZ (10 μM) selectively increased the postspike EPSP amplitude in pvBCs to 119.6 ± 3.3% from baseline (mean of means ± sem, p=0.0001, Student's t-test, n = 7 cells) (P of data points in individual experiments from 0.127 to 0.995, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) that had no effect on prespike EPSP amplitude (102.0 ± 1.6% of baseline, n = 7).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: GBZ had no effect on prespike EPSP amplitude in pvBCs.
source: Following baseline, wash-in of GBZ (10 μM) selectively increased the postspike EPSP amplitude in pvBCs to 119.6 ± 3.3% from baseline (mean of means ± sem, p=0.0001, Student's t-test, n = 7 cells) (P of data points in individual experiments from 0.127 to 0.995, Shapiro-Wilk normality test) that had no effect on prespike EPSP amplitude (102.0 ± 1.6% of baseline, n = 7).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: GBZ wash-in in nonFSINs failed to increase the prespike EPSP or postspike EPSP.
source: Similar experiments in nonFSINs (action inward current width 0.850 ± 0.041 ms in nonFSINs vs. 0.600 ± 0.031 in pvBCs, p=000193, t-test) failed to increase the prespike EPSP (amplitude 104.0 ± 1.5% of baseline) or postspike EPSP (amplitude 97.1 ± 4.0% of baseline) (n = 8).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments in nonFSINs.

claim: Wash-in of GBZ shortened the spike doublet interval in pvBCs.
source: First, we found that wash-in of GBZ shortened the spike doublet interval (Figure 5ai–ii), indicating GABAAR-mediated inhibition of the 2nd spike initiation in baseline conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Autaptic inhibitory conductance elongated the doublet spike interval in pvBCs.
source: We found that by the autaptic inhibitory conductance, the doublet spike interval was elongated (Figure 5bii,d) (ANOVA on ranks with Dunn's post hoc test) or the 2nd spike probability was reduced (Figure 5bii, c-d).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Autaptic inhibitory conductance reduced the 2nd spike probability in pvBCs.
source: We found that by the autaptic inhibitory conductance, the doublet spike interval was elongated (Figure 5bii,d) (ANOVA on ranks with Dunn's post hoc test) or the 2nd spike probability was reduced (Figure 5bii, c-d).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Applying 2.5 nS-10 nS autaptic inhibition by dynamic clamp reduced the 2nd spike probability in three experiments to 0.34 (median, quartiles 0.02–0.67) from 0.93 (median, quartiles 0.69–1.00) in 0 nS autapse conditions.
source: Applying 2.5 nS-10 nS autaptic inhibition by dynamic clamp reduced the 2nd spike probability in the three experiments to 0.34, 0.02–0.67 from 0.93, 0.69–1.00 in 0 nS autapse conditions (p=0.005, spike or no spike vs. 0 nS or 5–10 nS autapse, Chi-square test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: As low as 1 nS autapse was capable of reducing 2nd spike initiation.
source: Furthermore, as low as 1 nS autapse (tested in two of the cells) was capable of reducing 2nd spike initiation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Autaptic conductance measured in human pvBCs is sufficient to control spiking of the cells.
source: Thus, the results demonstrate that autaptic conductance measured in human pvBCs is sufficient to control spiking of the cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Studies on autapses in animal experiments have heavily focused on neurons in infragranular layers of the neocortex.
source: Furthermore, studies on autapses in animal experiments have heavily focused on neurons in infragranular layers of the neocortex, while the function of autapses in the supragranular layers has remained unexplored (Tamás et al., 1997; Bacci et al., 2003; Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Jiang et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement summarizes the focus of prior literature with citations.

claim: The function of autapses in the supragranular layers has remained unexplored.
source: Furthermore, studies on autapses in animal experiments have heavily focused on neurons in infragranular layers of the neocortex, while the function of autapses in the supragranular layers has remained unexplored (Tamás et al., 1997; Bacci et al., 2003; Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Jiang et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition is a regular feature of supragranular layer pvBCs in humans and mice.
source: Our study shows that GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition is a regular feature of supragranular layer pvBCs in humans and mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: pvBC axon terminals self-innervate their soma and proximal dendrites.
source: pvBC axon terminals self-innervate their soma and proximal dendrites, and electron microscopic investigation shows that these contacts form 'autaptic densities' in the interneurons.
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical analyses.

claim: Electron microscopic investigation shows that pvBC autaptic contacts form 'autaptic densities' in the interneurons.
source: pvBC axon terminals self-innervate their soma and proximal dendrites, and electron microscopic investigation shows that these contacts form 'autaptic densities' in the interneurons.
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy analysis.

claim: The regular occurrence of autapses in pvBCs in different species and different layers and areas of the neocortex shows that self-inhibition is a common but cell type-specific microcircuit feature in the mammalian neocortex.
source: The regular occurrence of autapses in pvBCs in different species and different layers and areas of the neocortex, their robust inhibitory efficacy in pvBCs and their rare occurrence in nonFSINs show that self-inhibition is a common but cell type-specific microcircuit feature in the mammalian neocortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Autapses efficiently control excitability in pvBCs after spikes.
source: Here, our results in the supragranular layer together with other studies in the infragranular layers show that autapses efficiently control excitability in pvBCs after spikes (Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Connelly and Lees, 2010; Jiang et al., 2012; Deleuze et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Autapses are present in similar proportions in pvBCs of superficial and deep neocortical layers.
source: Autapses are present in similar proportions and show comparable inhibitory efficacy in pvBCs of superficial and deep neocortical layers (see Bacci and Huguenard, 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Autapses show comparable inhibitory efficacy in pvBCs of superficial and deep neocortical layers.
source: Autapses are present in similar proportions and show comparable inhibitory efficacy in pvBCs of superficial and deep neocortical layers (see Bacci and Huguenard, 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Autapses have similar occurrence and strength in pvBCs in rodent and human brain slices.
source: In addition, our results here with human and mouse cells (together with earlier studies on rat neurons) confirm that autapses have similar occurrence and strength in pvBCs in rodent and human brain slices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Self-innervation is rare in human nonFSINs, similar to rodent nonFSINs.
source: Correspondingly, self-innervation is rare in human nonFSINs, similar to rodent nonFSINs (Bacci et al., 2003; Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data compared to prior literature.

claim: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance in human pvBCs is comparable to the synaptic inhibition these interneurons exert on neighboring layer 2/3 neurons.
source: GABAergic self-inhibition conductance in human pvBCs is comparable to the synaptic inhibition these interneurons exert on neighboring layer 2/3 neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: Autaptic terminals on pvBC are heavily perisomatic.
source: Autaptic terminals on pvBC are heavily perisomatic, whereas nonFSINs, when autapses are found in them, self-innervate their own dendrites (Tamás et al., 1997) akin to synaptic contacts made by these interneurons to other neurons (Favuzzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical analyses.

claim: NonFSINs, when autapses are found in them, self-innervate their own dendrites.
source: Autaptic terminals on pvBC are heavily perisomatic, whereas nonFSINs, when autapses are found in them, self-innervate their own dendrites (Tamás et al., 1997) akin to synaptic contacts made by these interneurons to other neurons (Favuzzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical analyses supported by citations.

claim: The incidence of autaptic connectivity can be influenced by resected axons of brain slices.
source: Our results in human neocortex shed more light on this, but it is worth keeping in mind that the incidence of autaptic connectivity, and hence the strength of autaptic inhibition particularly in dendrites can be influenced by resected axons of brain slices.
evidence: This is a caveat about the experimental approach.

claim: In pvBCs, perisomatic GABAergic self-inhibition overlaps with much stronger AHP potassium conductance.
source: In pvBCs, perisomatic GABAergic self-inhibition overlaps with much stronger AHP potassium conductance.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The autaptic conductance onset delay and late peak time make GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition highly influential during AHP conductance decay.
source: However, the autaptic conductance onset delay and late peak time make GABAAR-mediated self-inhibition highly influential during AHP conductance decay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data.

claim: Autaptic activity strengthens somatic inhibitory conductance up to ~10 ms following a spike.
source: In this way, the autaptic activity strengthens somatic inhibitory conductance up to ~10 ms following a spike.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data and modeling.

claim: Autaptic inhibition elongates the action potential interval through shunting inhibition in human pvBCs.
source: We demonstrated this using a single-cell model as well as dynamic clamp experiments and showed that autaptic inhibition elongates the action potential interval (Bacci and Huguenard, 2006; Connelly, 2014; Guo et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2016; Deleuze et al., 2019) through shunting inhibition in human pvBCs.
evidence: This is a finding from modeling and dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: GABAergic inhibition through shunting is particularly relevant in pvBCs since the GABAA reversal potential in these cells is often close to the resting membrane potential.
source: GABAergic inhibition through shunting is particularly relevant in pvBCs since the GABAA reversal potential in these cells is often close to the resting membrane potential (Verheugen et al., 1999; Connelly and Lees, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Perisomatic self-innervation in human and mouse pvBCs reinforces self-inhibition after a spike.
source: Overall, perisomatic self-innervation in human and mouse pvBCs reinforces self-inhibition after a spike.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Perisomatic self-innervation adjusts the pvBC firing interval and rhythmic inhibition from pvBCs to other neurons.
source: This process adjusts the pvBC firing interval and rhythmic inhibition from pvBCs to other neurons (Guo et al., 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2016; Deleuze et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Autaptic self-innervation strength shows substantial variability between individual pvBCs.
source: However, autaptic self-innervation strength shows substantial variability between individual pvBCs, and therefore it is likely that autaptic GABAergic contacts undergo activity-dependent plasticity which regulates their strength (Castillo et al., 2011; Donato et al., 2013; Griffen and Maffei, 2014; Lourenço et al., 2014; Lourenço et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with speculation about plasticity supported by citations.

claim: It is likely that autaptic GABAergic contacts undergo activity-dependent plasticity which regulates their strength.
source: However, autaptic self-innervation strength shows substantial variability between individual pvBCs, and therefore it is likely that autaptic GABAergic contacts undergo activity-dependent plasticity which regulates their strength (Castillo et al., 2011; Donato et al., 2013; Griffen and Maffei, 2014; Lourenço et al., 2014; Lourenço et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data variability and supported by citations to plasticity literature.

claim: Comparison of autapses or cell input resistance showed no difference between human and mouse pvBCs.
source: Comparison of autapses or cell input resistance showed no difference between human and mouse pvBCs.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between human and mouse data.

claim: Compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs exhibit a wide range of autapse conductance as well as cell input resistance.
source: However, close investigation of the data reveals that compared to mouse pvBCs, human pvBCs exhibit a wide range of autapse conductance as well as cell input resistance.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Cortical region specificity and patient gender and age may partly be behind the parameter variability in human pvBCs.
source: One potential explanation for this finding is human tissue material diversity. Thus, cortical region specificity and patient gender and age may partly be behind the parameter variability in human pvBCs.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of data variability.

claim: Human neocortical neurons often exhibit higher Rm than their rodent counterparts do.
source: However, among various cellular features characterized in human and in rodent neocortex (Blazquez-Llorca et al., 2010; Testa-Silva et al., 2010; Molnár et al., 2016; Szegedi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2018; Boldog et al., 2018; Goriounova et al., 2018; Kalmbach et al., 2018; Pruunsild and Bading, 2019), human neocortical neurons often exhibit higher Rm than their rodent counterparts do (Eyal et al., 2016; Poorthuis et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human neurons had individual cells showing clearly higher Rm than did those found in any of the mouse pvBCs.
source: Although our data here showed that human and mouse pvBC input resistance values were not different on average, human neurons had individual cells showing clearly higher Rm than did those found in any of the mouse pvBCs (Poorthuis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: AHP conductance was generally higher in mouse cells than in human cells.
source: In line with this result, we found that AHP conductance was generally higher in mouse cells than in human cells.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: High Rm needs less current to generate an equal amplitude potential.
source: High Rm needs less current to generate an equal amplitude potential.
evidence: This is a statement based on Ohm's law.

claim: Human pvBC showed a correlation between AHP peak conductance and membrane leak conductance.
source: Indeed, human pvBC showed a correlation between AHP peak conductance and membrane leak conductance.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: High Rm pvBCs in the human neocortex need smaller conductance for efficient inhibition than do pvBCs in mice.
source: Thus, high Rm pvBCs in the human neocortex need smaller conductance for efficient inhibition than do pvBCs in mice.
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Firing of pvBCs coordinates synchrony of neuronal networks in the cortex.
source: Firing of pvBCs coordinates synchrony of neuronal networks in the cortex (Hu and Jonas, 2014; Lu et al., 2017; Cardin, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Through robust autapses, pvBCs adjust their temporal firing interval and correspondingly set inhibition in their target neurons.
source: Through robust autapses, pvBCs adjust their temporal firing interval and correspondingly set inhibition in their target neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: pvBC self-inhibition may be essential in setting cell assembly discharges in the neocortex during associative memory processing and memory retrieval.
source: This mechanism may be essential in setting cell assembly discharges in the neocortex (Molnár et al., 2008; Tóth et al., 2018; de la Prida and Huberfeld, 2019) during associative memory processing (Kucewicz et al., 2014) and memory retrieval (Vaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role supported by citations.

claim: pvBC self-inhibition may contribute to pyramidal cell disinhibition during the induction of L2/3 long-term potentiation associated with learning.
source: In addition, pvBC self-inhibition may contribute to pyramidal cell disinhibition during the induction of L2/3 long-term potentiation associated with learning (Williams and Holtmaat, 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role supported by citation.
